SEC10A-01.struck_how: C and D put a colon directly after 'including' (no edited text does this). A puts a semicolon before an 'including' phrase, which is visibly not a clause. That leaves only the key without reading the passage.
SEC10A-01.fix: The options alone decide it. Replace the two colon distractors with ones that need the sentence to judge, e.g. 'objects—including hand-colored' (a dash opened and never closed before 'and a ledger'), or move the tested boundary to where the list ends.

SEC10A-02.struck_how: A has a comma between the verb and 'that'. B has a colon between the verb and a that-clause. C has a lone comma after 'that' with no interrupter. Each breaks a general rule visible in the option, so the bare option wins.
SEC10A-02.fix: The options alone decide it, and it uses the same template as SEC10A-10. Keep at most one of the two. To keep this one, the distractors must be locally legal, e.g. 'argued that, in a run of' paired with a passage where the interrupter's closing comma is missing, so that only reading the sentence decides it.

SEC10A-03.struck_how: No option breaks a rule on its own. 'which took', '; this took' and ', and it took' are each grammatical after some noun. Only the missing main verb for 'The decision' kills them, and you can see that only from the passage.

SEC10A-04.convention: B (commas around the name) is used only when the descriptor already picks out one person. Not the case for 'the Peruvian archaeologist', so B fails under Chicago and AP too.
SEC10A-04.struck_how: C opens a comma before the name and never closes it (an unclosed pair). D runs a 'whose' clause onto a proper name with no comma, and a nonrestrictive clause after a proper name is a general rule. Choosing between A and B then needs only the familiar 'no commas between title and name' pattern, so in practice the options alone decide it.
SEC10A-04.fix: Hard only in name. It is two textbook rules on one blank, laid out as a 2x2 grid (name commas yes/no × comma before 'whose' yes/no). To make it hard, use a descriptor that IS unique in context ('the expedition's only archaeologist, Rosa Quispe,'), so that the commas become correct and the student has to read for uniqueness.

SEC10A-05.struck_how: A puts a semicolon before 'and then compared', which has no subject. D starts a sentence with the subjectless 'Then compared'. Both are fragments visible in the option. B (comma + 'they') needs the passage to confirm the splice.
SEC10A-05.fix: Shares its frame with SEC10A-11 ('<noun> ; / , / . / bare + then compared'). Change one item's verb and option frame so the two are not visibly siblings.

SEC10A-06.struck_how: B and C both put a semicolon directly before a subjectless 'was'. D has a single comma after 'however', an unclosed interrupter pair. The key is the only option with a matched comma pair.
SEC10A-06.fix: The options alone decide it. Use distractors that are legal on their own and fail only in this sentence: 'south; however, it was far' (the part before the semicolon is a bare noun phrase) and 'south, however, it was far' (subject left with no verb). Keep the key.

SEC10A-07.struck_how: C ends with a comma after the subject 'the council,' and that comma pairs with nothing. A (splice) and B ('which' with no role) need the passage to confirm.
SEC10A-07.fix: C's trailing comma gives it away. Make C ', and by then the council' (correct by itself), and get the error from somewhere that needs the sentence, or replace C with a semicolon variant.

SEC10A-08.struck_how: B (inverted order + period) and C (statement order + question mark) are internally inconsistent, so no edited text uses them. That leaves the two consistent cells of a 2x2 grid (word order × end mark), and you need the passage to choose between them.
SEC10A-08.fix: Break the 2x2. Swap B for a statement-order option that is wrong for another reason, e.g. 'could have sank.', or an option that ends the clause without the verb.

SEC10A-09.struck_how: B puts a semicolon before a participle (a visible non-clause). D is ', this allows', a comma followed by a new subject and finite verb, the usual splice shape. C ('. Allowing') could in principle open a gerund-subject sentence, so strictly it needs the passage.
SEC10A-09.fix: Replace D with ', which allowed' (correct by itself, but here it agrees awkwardly and its antecedent is ambiguous) or with '—allowing', so the item can't be solved from the options alone.

SEC10A-10.struck_how: A has a comma after 'that'. C has a colon after 'that'. D has a comma between the verb and 'that'. Every distractor breaks a rule visible in the option, so the bare option wins. The option set is the same as SEC10A-02's.
SEC10A-10.fix: Drop it, because it duplicates SEC10A-02's template. The explanation also never quotes the options ('The choice with no punctuation at all', 'The choices that put a comma or a colon after that'); it should name each option in quotation marks as the other items do.

SEC10A-11.struck_how: A puts a semicolon before the subjectless 'then compared'. B starts a sentence with the subjectless 'Then compared'. D (no comma) needs the series context in the passage.
SEC10A-11.fix: Uses SEC10A-05's frame and even its verb ('then compared'), but the key flips: a bare join there, a comma here. Change the verb and the option frame, e.g. test the comma before 'and built' instead.

SEC10A-12.convention: An em dash ('recorded—the') would be equally correct under Chicago and AP, but none is offered, so the item stays exclusive.
SEC10A-12.struck_how: No option breaks a rule on its own. 'recorded the' is a normal verb + object, and ', and the' and '. The' are both normal. Only the passage shows that 'recorded' already has its object and that the noun phrase after it has no verb.

SEC10A-13.struck_how: Nothing can be struck strictly. B's comma looks misplaced ('over water rights federal mediators'), but judging it needs the phrase boundary. A single dash and a semicolon are both legal somewhere. In practice B is weak.
SEC10A-13.fix: B is a weak distractor. Replace it with 'states, over water rights, federal mediators' (paired commas, which look deliberate but cut the phrase in two) to make the item harder.

cross_item_tells: Strike every semicolon: 8 of 13 items carry a semicolon distractor (01, 03, 05, 06 [two], 09, 11, 13). The key contains a semicolon in 0 of 13. Applied blind, this heuristic removes at least one distractor on 8 items and never removes the key.

Two items on one template: 02 and 10 have the same option set (verb ± comma/colon around 'that'), and the bare option is the key in both. Every distractor in both can be struck from the options alone.
05 and 11 share a frame and a verb ('<noun> ; / , / . / bare + then compared'). The keys differ (bare 'and then' vs comma), so the pattern doesn't pick the key, but the two are visibly siblings.

Bare option (no punctuation) is the key in 4 of the 7 items that offer one (02, 03, 05, 10; wrong on 04, 11, 12), against 25% by chance. A 'pick the plainest option' heuristic decides 5 items outright (01, 02, 03, 05, 10, all correct), ties on 09 and 13, and is wrong on 04, 06, 07, 11, 12. So it is noticeably above chance, but not decisive.

2x2 grids where the two internally inconsistent cells strike themselves: 08 (word order × end mark), leaving 2 options. 04 is also a grid (title-name commas × comma before 'whose'), and there the general rules leave only the key.
Colon: a colon appears in 4 items (01 [two], 02, 10, 12) and is the key only in 12. 'Strike the colon' is right on 3 of 4 items and wrong on 12.
Key letters A4 B3 C3 D3, so there is no position tell.

summary: Keys: 13/13 matched my cold solve, and every item is exclusive. No second defensible option; the only alternative convention found is an em dash on 12, which isn't offered. All items are Boundaries and on the blueprint. 4 items are decided by the options alone (01, 02, 06, 10) and 02/10 share one template, so drop or rebuild those. Only 03 and 12 (n_struck 0, strong distractors) are real module-2 hard. The batch-wide tell is the semicolon: it is a distractor in 8 of 13 items and never in a key. Difficulty: easy 3 (01, 02, 10), medium 8 (04, 05, 06, 07, 08, 09, 11, 13), hard 2 (03, 12).
